one_liner: Dynamic language JIT-compiled through LLVM per concrete argument types; beats LuaJIT, PyPy and Node on loop-heavy CPU code.
what_it_does: Julia is a garbage-collected dynamic language for technical computing. Its runtime (C/C++ in src/, the compiler written in Julia) compiles each method the first time it is called with a new set of argument types. You get the speed by writing the program in Julia; it does not run Lua, Python or JavaScript. C and C++ hosts can embed it through libjulia (`jl_init`, `jl_eval_string`, `jl_call`), and Julia calls C or Fortran directly through `ccall`.
how_it_is_fast: When a function is first called with a given set of argument types, type inference (Compiler/src/typeinfer.jl) bounds every variable's type. It also does constant propagation and inlining. Codegen (codegen.cpp) then emits LLVM IR that LLVM optimizes to native code. This is method specialization driven by multiple dispatch, with no tracing and no deoptimization tier, so type-stable code with concrete-typed arrays compiles much like C. Users can add `@inbounds`, `@simd` and `@fastmath` to drop bounds checks and allow SIMD vectorization and floating-point reassociation. Since 1.9, precompiled packages store native code in pkgimages, which cuts warm-up.
when_to_use: Numeric loops over Float64 arrays, written as plain loops: plb2 matmul (1500x1500, Apple M1) took 0.76 s, against 1.14 s for OpenJDK 20, 2.66 s for LuaJIT 2.1, 2.88 s for Node 21.5 and 4.89 s for PyPy 7.3.14.
Branchy integer and bit-twiddling search: plb2 nqueen took 3.02 s (Java 3.92, LuaJIT 5.31, PyPy 6.91) and sudoku 2.18 s (Java 3.20, LuaJIT 4.48, PyPy 8.82).
Jobs that run for seconds or longer, where compile time is amortized: kostya's brainfuck interpreter on bench.b took 1.564 s, against 2.954 s for Node.js, 5.686 s for LuaJIT and 9.398 s for PyPy.
Replacing Python or NumPy prototypes in scientific code with one language that calls C and Fortran libraries without wrapper code.
Adding a numeric scripting layer to a C or C++ application, provided you can accept a heavy runtime: libjulia exposes jl_init, jl_eval_string and jl_call.
when_not_to_use: Short-lived scripts and CLI tools: every process compiles on first call. Kostya measured a 244 MB base RSS against 2.5 MB for LuaJIT, and plb2 notes JIT runtimes can spend up to about 0.3 s compiling and warming up.

String, byte and JSON-heavy workloads: in kostya's runs, base64 took 3.085 s (Node 0.635 s, Java 1.435 s), JSON with JSON3 0.700 s (Node 0.374 s) and primes 0.680 s (Java 0.161 s, LuaJIT 0.309 s, PyPy 0.617 s).
When OpenJDK HotSpot is the bar for interpreter-style code: on kostya's runs Java took 1.191 s on bench.b against Julia's 1.564 s, and 13.041 s on mandel.b against 30.315 s.

Type-unstable code (untyped globals, abstract-typed containers or fields): the Performance Tips manual says this blocks inference and adds allocation, and speed falls back toward dynamic-language levels.

Hosts that call into the runtime from arbitrary threads, or that need a small embeddable VM: the C API requires jl_init exactly once and allows jl_ calls only from that thread or from threads Julia started.

integration.form: language runtime: the `julia` executable, plus the libjulia shared library and julia.h for embedding (julia-config.jl prints the cflags, ldflags and ldlibs)
integration.dependencies: Prebuilt binaries bundle a patched LLVM (master pins LLVM 22.1.8 in deps/llvm.version), OpenBLAS and other libraries. Building from source needs gcc/g++ 7.1+ or Clang 5.0+, gfortran, libatomic, cmake, python3 and perl.
integration.min_toolchain: Building: gcc 7.1+ or Clang 5.0+ (Apple Clang 9.3+). Embedding: any C/C++ compiler that links libjulia. kostya ran Julia 1.11.6 and plb2 ran 1.10.0.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD; x86-64, ARM (aarch64) and RISC-V have build notes. Support tiers are on julialang.org (not opened).
integration.thread_safety: The language has multithreading (tasks, Threads.@threads). The embedding C API is 'not fully thread-safe': jl_init may be called once, and jl_ functions only from that thread or from threads the Julia runtime started.

gotchas: Harness flaw in the kostya matmul row: 'Julia (no BLAS)' (1.113 s) runs a column-major saxpy loop with `@simd ivdep` and `@fastmath`, while Java (3.057 s) and C/gcc (3.034 s) transpose b and run a strict-IEEE dot-product reduction that cannot vectorize. Plain C matches Java, so the 2.7x reflects loop shape and fast-math, not the runtime. Plb2's like-for-like matmul gives 1.5x over Java (0.76 s vs 1.14 s).

Kostya runs Julia with `--check-bounds=no`. Core developer Keno Fischer (open issue #48245, 'Consider removing --check-bounds=no?') calls the flag unsafe and says it can make code 'significantly' slower by disabling concrete evaluation in inference. The published numbers therefore come from a non-default, discouraged setting, and default runs may be faster or slower.

Kostya's timer starts after the notify() call, after a verify() run on the same functions, so most JIT compile time is excluded. Plb2 includes start-up and compile time and reports wall-clock time; its README notes Julia uses noticeably more CPU time than wall time even on nqueen.

Kostya's bf.jl is a weaker algorithm than the Java and Node ports: it matches brackets by scanning raw characters at run time, where they parse an op tree first. Julia's bench.b win over Node, LuaJIT and PyPy holds despite that, but this row compares code shapes, not only runtimes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Julia over the Dart VM or Chez Scheme for numeric and array code: plb2 matmul 0.76 s vs Dart 2.74 s and Chez 9.5.8 at 18.98 s. Julia also beat Dart on all four plb2 tasks. Pick the .NET runtime (CoreCLR) instead for interpreter-style or object-heavy code and when start-up and memory matter: on kostya bench.b C#/.NET took 1.280 s vs Julia's 1.564 s with 37 MB vs 244 MB base RSS, and .NET 8 NativeAOT beat Julia on plb2 nqueen, sudoku and bedcov but not matmul (1.38 s vs 0.76 s).
verified_claims_summary: Two public cross-language suites agree on the direction. In kostya/benchmarks (Julia 1.11.6 with `--optimize=3 --check-bounds=no`, Intel Xeon E-2324G, Docker on Debian, medians), the brainfuck bench.b ran in 1.564 s, against Node.js v26.5.0 at 2.954 s, LuaJIT 2.1 at 5.686 s and PyPy 7.3.23 at 9.398 s, while Java 24 was faster at 1.191 s. In plb2 (hyperfine wall-clock time on an Apple M1, Julia 1.10.0), Julia beat Java 20, Node 21.5, LuaJIT 2.1 and PyPy 7.3.14 on nqueen, matmul, sudoku and bedcov.
status_note: Very active (MIT, 49.2k stars, 3.7k open issues, master at 1.14-dev with commits on 2026-10-06) and production-grade. You adopt it as a whole language and runtime rather than vendoring code, and its wins are limited to loop- and array-heavy code.
